# WaveStar NMPC source reference convergence diagnostic

The first 4,501-sample, independent 225 s MATLAB R2025b WaveStar NMPC
step diagnostic came from [Python-repository CI run
39883276159](https://github.com/cmudrc/wec-sim-python/actions/runs/39883276159)
and its [repeat run
39886232300](https://github.com/cmudrc/wec-sim-python/actions/runs/39886232300).
The `source_*.npz` files also preserve compact traces from the later runs
documented below. They are **diagnostics, not accepted physical parity
references**. Each initial run's
three source artifacts contain the original body/PTO CSV files and controller MAT
files. `convergence.json` and `convergence_rerun.json` record the full
source-to-source comparisons in the two runs.

The workflow pins WEC-Sim `0753b2e47f2457c078751dcfe5d251d1767b80ab`,
Applications `d53d4d4c9eda2581f04204f5d394a6ef84bb099e`, and the exact
`wavestar.h5` in
[`../wavestar_nmpc_split_step_225s`](../wavestar_nmpc_split_step_225s/README.md)
(SHA-256 `b2541ff01c319987d9157d1be9fbc9ec39a7660d0572d8e316c428b8aa3359d1`).
The 500 wave components match that pinned fixture exactly. The first runs use
the `ode4` source plant, the same 50 ms controller and output interval, and
plant steps of 1, 0.5, or 0.25 ms. Later runs refine the step further, as
described below. Only disposable Applications input files were
configured for the runs; no changes were pushed to either MATLAB repository.
The NPZ arrays are float64 copies of exported source time, pitch, pitch
speed, PTO stroke and speed, axial force, requested torque, and components.

| Comparison | Max pitch gap | Max request gap |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Older pinned 1 ms vs fresh 1 ms | 0.010596 rad | 0.792728 N m |
| Fresh 1 ms vs 0.5 ms | 0.009193 rad | 0.573686 N m |
| Fresh 0.5 ms vs 0.25 ms | 0.004763 rad | 0.450018 N m |
| First vs repeated 0.25 ms | 0.012014 rad | 0.732573 N m |

The original pointwise limits are 0.0005 rad pitch and 0.1 N m request.
The older and fresh 1 ms source pitches agree to `2.29e-15` rad through
15.2 s, then separate after NMPC activation. The first 15.2 s pitch gaps
between the fresh 1/0.5 and 0.5/0.25 ms runs are `2.6722e-5` and
`1.3348e-5` rad; smaller plant steps have not delivered an acceptable full
closed-loop target. Independent physical Python, run at the matching plant
step with only the exact HDF5 and generated sea phases driving feedback,
differs from the 0.5/0.25 ms source traces by up to 0.006714/0.009435 rad
pitch. The 0.25 ms pitch-peak aggregate gap is 0.7149%, over its 0.5% limit.
These first matched-step Python checks ran locally on macOS ARM64 with NumPy
2.5.4 and SciPy 1.18.1. In the repeat Linux run, the two 1 ms and two 0.5 ms
source exports reproduced exactly at their respective steps. The 0.25 ms
source exports agree within `1.10e-15` rad pitch through 15.2 s, but differ
by up to `0.012014` rad pitch and `0.732573` N m request over 225 s despite
the same HDF5 hash, sea components, source revisions, and step settings.
The repeated 0.25 ms source is `source_0p25ms_repeat.npz`; its matching Linux
Python pitch gap is `0.011711` rad and the pitch-peak aggregate gap is
`0.7851%`. Both exceed the original limits. The earlier pinned 1 ms trace
also differs from both standalone 1 ms runs, although those standalone runs
match each other numerically. This record does not isolate which runner or
source setup detail caused the difference.

A [single-thread repeat](https://github.com/cmudrc/wec-sim-python/actions/runs/39891127477)
held [MATLAB's computational thread limit](https://www.mathworks.com/help/matlab/ref/maxnumcompthreads.html)
at one in two fresh 0.25 ms runs. Both used R2025b Update 7, the exact HDF5,
the same sea components, and identical source revisions. The Intel Xeon
Platinum 8573C run reproduced `source_0p25ms_repeat.npz` exactly; the AMD EPYC
9V45 run reproduced `source_0p25ms.npz` exactly. Their pitch and request gaps
remain `0.012014` rad and `0.732573` N m. The matched independent Python
pitch gaps are `0.011711` and `0.006740` rad respectively, both beyond the
pointwise limit. [`single_thread_repeat.json`](single_thread_repeat.json)
records the numerical comparison, MATLAB versions and thread counts, and
runner CPU details. This associates the two source trajectories with the
tested CPU models despite one MATLAB computational thread; it does not
identify the exact CPU-dependent operation.

The two single-thread controller logs also permit a 0–40 s frozen-input
probe. [`single_thread_controller_probe.json`](single_thread_controller_probe.json)
was generated by
[`wavestar_nmpc_controller_source_probe.py`](../../../../tools/wavestar_nmpc_controller_source_probe.py),
feeding each source's logged observer states and AR forecast to an independent
Python QP. Its maximum Python-versus-corresponding-source request gaps are
`0.000136` and `0.000085` N m. The two source requests themselves separate by
`0.196588` N m within 40 s, and the two Python replays reproduce that
separation to within `8.84e-8` N m at its 39.55 s maximum. This rules out a
large Python QP replay mismatch in this early window; it does not identify
which upstream floating-point operation first perturbs the closed loop. The
logged AR forecasts already differ by up to `17.77` N m at 10.4 s, during the
resistive startup interval when the forecast does not drive the command.

A [compatible-BLAS repeat](https://github.com/cmudrc/wec-sim-python/actions/runs/39894739858)
then used [MathWorks' MATLAB override](https://www.mathworks.com/matlabcentral/answers/2066506-how-do-i-make-matlab-use-the-mkl_cbwr-environment-variable-as-the-cnr-branch)
and [Intel's common code branch](https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/docs/onemkl/developer-reference-c/2026-0/getting-started-with-conditional-numerical.html).
Both source jobs reported R2025b Update 7, one computational thread, and
oneMKL 2024.1's `CNR branch compatible` in `version -blas`. Both happened to
run on AMD EPYC 7763. Their full 225 s exported pitch, speed, stroke, force,
and request traces match numerically exactly; the compact
[`source_0p25ms_compatible_amd7763.npz`](source_0p25ms_compatible_amd7763.npz)
and [`compatible_repeat_summary.json`](compatible_repeat_summary.json)
preserve that result and its audit. This is a same-CPU repeat, so it does not
show that compatible BLAS removes the Intel/AMD source difference. The
[`compatible_controller_probe.json`](compatible_controller_probe.json) also
finds identical logged observer states, AR forecasts, and source requests
through 40 s; Python's frozen-input QP request stays within `0.000012` N m
of each source. The
independent physical Python run at the same 0.25 ms plant step misses every
pointwise limit: its maximum pitch gap is `0.017938` rad versus `0.0005`
rad, and its requested-torque gap is `0.937424` N m versus `0.1` N m. The
pitch-peak aggregate gap is `0.6762%` versus `0.5%`. This source can be used
to diagnose the Python discrepancy on that CPU, but it is not an accepted
portable physical parity baseline.

A further [compatible-BLAS run](https://github.com/cmudrc/wec-sim-python/actions/runs/39950081356)
used two AMD EPYC 9V45 runners, with the same pinned inputs, MATLAB release,
single-thread setting, and reported compatible oneMKL branch. Both generated
identical 225 s source traces. Comparing either with the earlier AMD EPYC 7763
compatible source also gives exactly zero pitch, pitch-speed, stroke, force,
and requested-torque difference at all 4,501 saved samples; the
[`cross-model report`](compatible_cross_amd_models.json) records the comparison.
This establishes
source repeatability across those two tested AMD CPU models. At that stage,
Intel and Apple silicon source portability remained unverified. The
independently running Python physical loop still fails all five pointwise
limits on the EPYC 9V45 runners:
maximum pitch `0.006638` rad and requested torque `0.561726` N m. Both CPU
groups used NumPy 2.5.4 and SciPy 1.18.1, yet their autonomous Python
trajectories differ. The matching checked source trace does not remove
Python closed-loop numerical sensitivity.

The [physical startup refinement](physical_startup_refinement_mac_arm.json),
reproduced by
[`wavestar_nmpc_startup_refinement.py`](../../../../tools/wavestar_nmpc_startup_refinement.py),
runs the independent physical Python path through NMPC activation at 15 s
against the checked 0.25 ms source. Refining only Python's plant step from
1 ms to 0.0625 ms changes the maximum startup pitch gap by less than
`2.0e-12` rad; it remains `1.06414e-5` rad. The command gap through 15 s
remains `0.00320464` N m. The physical Python startup is already converged
at these steps relative to this fixed source trace. Further Python RK4 step
refinement alone cannot remove the mismatch that enters NMPC feedback.

Two [native Apple silicon source runs](https://github.com/cmudrc/wec-sim-python/actions/runs/39954652940)
on macOS 15 with MATLAB R2025b Update 7, one computational thread, and
Apple Accelerate BLAS generated identical 225 s traces. The checked compact
[`source_0p25ms_macos_arm_m1.npz`](source_0p25ms_macos_arm_m1.npz)
(SHA-256 `b7c09d34fa247a897ac55ad3d7d4cd8251b679ed55ec01c3d4155b17d072a3d6`)
can be regenerated from either artifact with
[`wavestar_nmpc_compact_source.py`](../../../../tools/wavestar_nmpc_compact_source.py).
It is a platform-specific diagnostic, not an accepted physical parity
reference. Against the checked AMD compatible source, the Apple source differs
by up to `0.006697` rad pitch and `0.472857` N m request, beyond the
original pointwise limits. The independent physical Python run against its
own Apple source still misses all five limits, including `0.005875` rad
pitch and `0.542261` N m request. Its pitch-peak aggregate gap is `0.6555%`,
over the original `0.5%` aggregate limit. The
[`macOS source comparison`](macos_arm_source_comparison.json) records the
full pointwise, aggregate, and 40 s controller probes. The two sources'
commands agree within `8.2e-14` N m at NMPC activation, then separate by
`0.145978` N m
at 39.55 s; Python QP replays on each source's logged inputs reproduce that
separation to within `5.8e-8` N m. This supports feedback amplification of
small platform numerical differences, while the startup AR fit also has a
separate transient forecast difference before NMPC activation.

Two further [Apple silicon source jobs](https://github.com/cmudrc/wec-sim-python/actions/runs/39992588386)
halved the plant step to 0.125 ms while retaining the pinned sea, 50 ms
controller, and 225 s duration. Their compact
[`source_0p125ms_macos_arm_m1.npz`](source_0p125ms_macos_arm_m1.npz)
traces are byte-identical; the [corrected archived repeat
comparison](https://github.com/cmudrc/wec-sim-python/actions/runs/39999436632)
passes with zero differences in pitch, speed, stroke, force, and request.
The original workflow's compare job failed because its earlier comparator
hardcoded 0.25 ms; both source and physical audit jobs succeeded, and the
corrected comparator was rerun on those same artifacts. The
[`half-step comparison`](macos_arm_half_step_source_comparison.json) shows
that the 0.125 and 0.25 ms Apple source traces themselves differ by up to
`0.006753` rad pitch and `0.687034` N m request; their pitch-peak aggregate
gap is `0.5691%`, above the original `0.5%` limit. The independent physical
Python run at the matching 0.125 ms step still misses all five pointwise
limits, including `0.006806` rad pitch against `0.0005` and `0.434049` N m
request against `0.1`. All seven aggregates pass. Refining the source and
Python plant steps together therefore does not meet the unchanged autonomous
gate. This finer trace remains a diagnostic, not an accepted parity target.

Two more [Apple silicon source jobs](https://github.com/cmudrc/wec-sim-python/actions/runs/40006669298)
halved the plant step again to 0.0625 ms. Both use the same pinned HDF5 and
wave phases, MATLAB R2025b Update 7, Apple Accelerate BLAS, one computational
thread, and the 50 ms controller for all 225 s. Their five source channels
match exactly at all 4,501 samples; packing either artifact produces the
byte-identical
[`source_0p0625ms_macos_arm_m1.npz`](source_0p0625ms_macos_arm_m1.npz)
(SHA-256 `b3fe52fe66256a218c924c1c039f60c4b3d9d2192f36b1d9d4efe56831fac26b`).
The [repeat report](macos_arm_quarter_step_repeat.json) preserves this check.
The [step comparison](macos_arm_quarter_step_source_comparison.json) shows
that the 0.125 and 0.0625 ms *MATLAB source* traces differ by up to
`0.010800` rad pitch and `0.721063` N m request. Pitch first crosses the
unchanged `0.0005` rad pointwise limit at 17.95 s, although all seven
aggregate source-to-source gaps are below `0.5%`.
On each source's logged observer states and AR forecast, a separate Python
controller replay stays within `3.01e-6` N m of the source request through
40 s; its [probe report](macos_arm_quarter_step_controller_probe.json)
also shows exact agreement between the two MATLAB repeats. This is a
fixed-input component check, not autonomous parity.

The matching independent physical Python audit at experimental commit
[`7d4824d`](https://github.com/cmudrc/wec-sim-python/commit/7d4824d8a96baa0e6f6804308379f4f6efc1c1a0)
includes the source's light BC rod and motor bodies. It still misses all five
pointwise limits: `0.008512` rad pitch, `0.040802` rad/s pitch speed,
`0.001701` m stroke, `3.1800` N axial force, and `0.659784` N m request.
Its pitch-peak aggregate gap is `0.8871%`, above the unchanged `0.5%` limit.
The auxiliary-body correction also fails the existing 1 ms aggregate test,
so it was not merged. The checked source trace and these failed audits are
diagnostics, not an accepted physical parity baseline. Issue
[#623](https://github.com/cmudrc/wec-sim-python/issues/623) remains open.

Two [native Intel macOS source runs](https://github.com/cmudrc/wec-sim-python/actions/runs/39954640642)
on the `macos-15-intel` runner with MATLAB R2025b Update 7, one computational
thread, and oneMKL 2023.2.2 with CNR off also generated identical 225 s
traces. Both independently packed copies of
[`source_0p25ms_macos_intel.npz`](source_0p25ms_macos_intel.npz)
have SHA-256 `3c7596c0f39bb51bf3836802643597c827bac1ecb2cb6d625669a897baad92ef`.
The Intel source differs from the checked compatible AMD source by up to
`0.006825` rad pitch and `0.507981` N m request, and from the Apple source by
up to `0.007742` rad pitch and `0.624313` N m request. These are all beyond
the original pointwise limits, although the three source traces agree to
roughly `2e-15` rad pitch through 15.2 s. The
[`Intel source comparison`](macos_intel_source_comparison.json) records both
full-duration physical Python audits. They miss every pointwise limit: pitch
gaps are `0.007962` and `0.007568` rad, and request gaps are `0.722569` and
`0.605466` N m. All seven aggregate gaps pass on both Intel runners. A 40 s
controller probe finds the AMD and Intel source commands only `6.4e-14` N m
apart at NMPC activation but `0.082210` N m apart at 38.65 s. Python QP
replays on each logged input reproduce that later command separation within
`6.9e-8` N m. The native Intel trace is a diagnostic, not an accepted
physical parity reference.

The [prescribed-request physical component audit](compatible_prescribed_physical.json)
holds the same source's torque requests with the source's one-sample actuator
delay and independently advances the physical Python plant for 225 s. On
macOS ARM64 at the matching 0.25 ms plant step, the maximum pitch, pitch-speed,
PTO-stroke, and axial-force gaps are `0.0000625` rad, `0.000368` rad/s,
`0.0000125` m, and `0.000962` N. All four pass their original pointwise
limits; PTO work differs by `0.0233%`. The
[`wavestar_nmpc_prescribed_reference_audit.py`](../../../../tools/wavestar_nmpc_prescribed_reference_audit.py)
tool reproduces the check, and the ordinary Python parity workflow runs this
component gate on Linux x86 and Apple silicon. It deliberately feeds the
saved source request, so it does not satisfy the autonomous feedback gate.

The two compatible-BLAS source jobs also exported identical observer states,
AR forecasts, and requested torques at all 4,501 controller samples. Their
checked compact [controller signals](controller_0p25ms_compatible_amd7763.npz)
and [full replay report](compatible_controller_components.json) allow the
[`wavestar_nmpc_reference_controller_audit.py`](../../../../tools/wavestar_nmpc_reference_controller_audit.py)
tool to replay the observer, predictor, and QP without requiring an expiring
workflow artifact. On the source stroke and preceding source requests, the
Python observer differs by at most `1.75e-12` in its five states. The AR
forecast differs by at most `2.77e-11` N m during active NMPC; its larger
`4.70` N m difference occurs at 10.4 s, before the forecast drives requests.
The complete Python request replay differs by at most `0.001071` N m and
`0.0000336` N m RMS, passing the existing `0.01` and `0.0003` N m component
limits. Replaying the QP on the *source's own* logged states and forecasts
still gives a `0.001071` N m peak difference. Thus the active observer and
predictor replay are not the source of this fixed-input request gap; a small
QP numerical difference remains and can be amplified in autonomous feedback.
The portable Python CI now gates this controller component on Linux x86 and
Apple silicon separately from the autonomous run.

A further [direct QP replay](https://github.com/cmudrc/wec-sim-python/actions/runs/39905055593)
called the pinned Applications `NMPC.m` on all 4,201 active states and
forecasts in the checked compatible controller log. It used the checked
`A`, `Bu`, `Bw`, and `R` matrices from the earlier direct-controller fixture,
with MATLAB R2025b, one computational thread, and compatible BLAS. The
resulting full 40-step plans are preserved in
[`checked_qp_replay_compatible_amd7763.mat`](checked_qp_replay_compatible_amd7763.mat).
Its first commands reproduce the source simulation's requests within
`6.43e-11` N m over 15–225 s. Thus the direct source QP replay is an
independent check of the logged source controller inputs and command timing.

The [platform-fixed QP replay](fixed_input_qp_platform_comparison.json) uses
those same 4,201 states, forecasts, and matrices on compatible-BLAS Linux,
native Intel macOS, and native Apple silicon macOS. All three MATLAB runs
reproduce the checked source requests within `6.43e-11` N m. Their complete
40-step plans differ across platforms by at most `1.68e-10` N m and their
first commands by at most `8.75e-11` N m. The linked
[Linux](https://github.com/cmudrc/wec-sim-python/actions/runs/39963460737),
[Intel](https://github.com/cmudrc/wec-sim-python/actions/runs/39963448239), and
[Apple silicon](https://github.com/cmudrc/wec-sim-python/actions/runs/39963448268)
workflow runs record each MATLAB release, thread count, and native BLAS.
The first Apple job could not acquire a hosted runner; its second attempt
succeeded. These fixed-input QP differences are many orders smaller than the
autonomous source gaps. They do not establish which upstream calculation first
perturbs feedback, or make the independent physical Python gate pass.

The [fixed-input AR replay](fixed_input_ar_platform_comparison.json) calls the
pinned Applications `predictor.m` on the same checked 4,501-sample estimated
excitation sequence on [compatible Linux](https://github.com/cmudrc/wec-sim-python/actions/runs/39995149681),
[native Intel macOS](https://github.com/cmudrc/wec-sim-python/actions/runs/39995153765),
and [native Apple silicon](https://github.com/cmudrc/wec-sim-python/actions/runs/39995157574).
All use MATLAB R2025b Update 7 and one computational thread. Linux reproduces
the checked forecast exactly. Intel and Apple forecasts differ from it by at
most `2.75e-12` and `2.84e-12` N m during active NMPC (15–225 s). Their
larger `0.00883` and `0.00748` N m differences occur at 10.4 s, before the
forecast drives commands; the next integer-second AR refit removes that
transient. At activation, replaying the different platform source
estimated-moment histories through the same Python predictor produces
`2.73e-12`/`5.08e-12` N m Intel/Apple forecast gaps from the AMD history,
compared with `3.40e-12`/`5.72e-12` N m in the source logs. This points to
the already different estimated-moment histories as the main initial active
predictor perturbation. It does not identify the upstream floating-point
operation or establish autonomous physical parity.

The [Python comparison](compatible_checked_qp_replay.json), reproduced by
[`wavestar_nmpc_checked_qp_replay.py`](../../../../tools/wavestar_nmpc_checked_qp_replay.py),
finds a `0.001071` N m maximum request gap and `0.002058` N m maximum
40-step plan gap when each solver carries its own plan. If Python starts each
QP from the *preceding MATLAB plan*, the next request and complete plan
instead differ by at most `1.76e-7` N m on the recorded macOS ARM run.
The large fixed-input replay gap therefore accumulates in the persistent
nominal-plan recursion; it is not a comparably large one-step QP discrepancy.
The largest isolated one-step difference occurs at 97.25 s: MATLAB returns
`-11.999999823863` N m while Python returns the exact `-12` N m lower bound.
The MATLAB source uses `quadprog` with its documented default
[`interior-point-convex` algorithm](https://www.mathworks.com/help/optim/ug/quadprog.html),
whereas Python uses L-BFGS-B. This bound slack explains that sample's
`1.76e-7` N m gap; it does not establish a full-loop correction.
This result identifies the remaining Python controller numerical defect more
precisely, but the autonomous full-duration physical gate still fails.

The Python repository's
[`wavestar-nmpc-reference-convergence.yml`](../../../../.github/workflows/wavestar-nmpc-reference-convergence.yml)
regenerates the MATLAB exports, audits autonomous physical Python, and
compares the source traces. A source target that passes across supported CPU
classes, a step-convergence argument, and a passing independent physical
pointwise gate are still required before issue #623 can close.
